z-m-24-01.title: One line of the solution erased a solution
z-m-24-01.topic: Solutions that disappear when both sides of an equation are divided by the same expression
z-m-24-01.goal: Find in which line of the solution a solution disappeared, generalize the conditions of equations where this happens, and make equations of your own that lose a solution and explain the reason.
z-m-24-01.material: Jia solved the equation x³ = 4x and wrote "the solutions are 2 and −2, two of them". Doyun looked at Jia's solution and only said it was different from his own answer, without giving a reason. In this task, all x are real numbers. (x³ is read as "x cubed" and x² is read as "x squared".)
z-m-24-01.thinking.0: Finding where the error is in a solution
z-m-24-01.thinking.1: Judging the conditions under which transforming an expression changes the set of solutions
z-m-24-01.thinking.2: Making counterexamples (equations that lose a solution) yourself
z-m-24-01.prereq.0: H2 in this batch is a division of difficulty and support level and does not mean the grade taught at school. Assumed school order: you learned in middle school how to solve quadratic equations by factoring, and met factoring of cubic expressions in Common Math.
z-m-24-01.prereq.1: A method of plugging a value into an equation to check whether both sides are equal
z-m-24-01.prereq.2: All x in this task are real numbers.
z-m-24-01.s.s1.prompt: This is Jia's solution. Choose the line that made the solution wrong, or the line where that mistake shows up as it is.
z-m-24-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, check one by one "is it an equation with the same solutions as the line just before it?"
z-m-24-01.s.s1.hint.1: Plug in 0, 2, −2 for x in turn and check whether the original equation x³ = 4x holds.
z-m-24-01.s.s1.line.0: Solve x³ = 4x. (x is a real number)
z-m-24-01.s.s1.line.1: Dividing both sides by x gives x² = 4.
z-m-24-01.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the solutions of this equation are 2 and −2, two of them.
z-m-24-01.s.s1.explain: In line 2 we divided by x, but if you plug x = 0 into the original equation, both sides are 0, so it holds. The case x = 0 was not looked at separately, so the solution 0 was left out, and that result led to the "two" in line 5. Lines 3 and 4 correctly solved the equation after dividing. The real solutions of the original equation are the three, −2, 0, 2.
z-m-24-01.s.s2.prompt: All the equations below are solved over the real numbers. Which one loses none of the solutions of the original equation even if you divide both sides by the expression given in parentheses or in the description and solve only the remaining equation?
z-m-24-01.s.s2.hint.0: For each equation, look for whether there is a value of x that makes the expression you want to divide by equal to 0.
z-m-24-01.s.s2.hint.1: Plug the values you found into both sides of the original equation, and also look at whether there is an equation for which no such real number exists at all.
z-m-24-01.s.s2.r.a: This is a choice that did not check what happens to both sides when you plug in the value that makes x − 2 equal to 0 into the original equation.
z-m-24-01.s.s2.r.b: You missed that the value that makes the divisor 0 may be a solution of the original equation. Plug in x = 0.
z-m-24-01.s.s2.r.c: This is a choice that worked it out by using as the criterion whether there is a real number that makes the divisor 0.
z-m-24-01.s.s2.r.d: Even if there is a square, at the value where x − 1 is 0, both sides are 0. Check whether that value is a solution.
z-m-24-01.s.s2.explain: If both sides have the form f·g = f·h, a value where f is 0 is always a solution. So if there is a real number where f is 0, you must take care of that value separately before dividing. x² + 3 is at least 3 for any real number, so it is never 0, and in c you do not lose a solution (x = 4) by dividing. If the range is widened to the complex numbers, the solutions of x² + 3 = 0 must also be considered, so the situation is different.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different equations of the form (x − a)(x − b) = c(x − a). a, b, c are integers from −9 to 9 and c ≠ 0. Make the solution that divides both sides by x − a lose one solution, with the lost solution a negative and the solution b + c obtained after dividing positive.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.hint.0: First choose a to be negative, and then try changing b and c so that b + c is positive.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.hint.1: Check what happens when you plug x = a into both sides of the equation you made.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.ok.c1: a, b, c are all integers.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.fail.c1: a, b, c must be integers.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.ok.c2: All three numbers are from −9 to 9.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.fail.c2: a, b, c must be from −9 to 9.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.ok.c4: The lost solution a is negative.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.ok.c5: The solution b + c obtained after dividing is positive.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.explain: For example, if a = −3, b = 1, c = 2, then (x + 3)(x − 1) = 2(x + 3). Dividing by x + 3 gives only x = 3, but x = −3 also makes both sides 0, so it is a solution. Moving everything to one side gives (x + 3)(x − 3) = 0, so the solutions are the two, −3 and 3. Equations whose solution a and the solution b + c obtained after dividing are the same count as one, so if these two are different, they are different equations.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.prompt: Choose one of the equations you made and write which solution (in numbers) disappears when both sides are divided by x − a, and the reason.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.hint.0: Calculate what each side becomes when you plug x = a into the equation you made.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.hint.1: Compare side by side the solution obtained with the expression after dividing and the solution obtained by moving everything to one side.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.placeholder: Example: The expression I made is ...
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check with the numbers in your example that plugging the disappearing solution into the original equation makes both sides equal?
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write the reason "the value that makes the divisor 0" in your own words?
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think of at least one way to find all the solutions without dividing (for example, moving everything to one side and making it a product)?
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.model.0: The expression I made is (x+3)(x−1)=2(x+3). If I divide by x+3, only x=3 is left, but if I plug in x=−3, both sides are 0, so −3 is also a solution. It is the value that makes the divisor 0, so the solution is lost.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.model.1: In (x+1)(x−4)=−1(x+1), dividing by x+1 gives only x−4=−1, that is, x=3. But if x=−1, x+1 is 0 and both sides are equal, so −1 is also a solution, and it disappears because it is the same as dividing by 0.
z-m-24-01.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: It is also good that it first said the solution obtained after dividing and then said the solution that disappeared.

z-m-24-02.title: How many solutions does a problem with no range have?
z-m-24-02.topic: The number of solutions of the cubic equation x³ = 1 and the range of numbers
z-m-24-02.goal: Work out which range of numbers a solution assumes, keep or revise your judgment about the number of solutions each time new information comes in, and confirm with an answer that depends on the range and with solutions you find yourself.
z-m-24-02.material: There is a problem of finding the solutions of the equation x³ = 1. The range of x is not written in the problem. Minsu wrote a solution that compares sizes, and Seoyun, who saw the solution, asked, "Shouldn't we decide the range first?" Information is revealed one piece at a time, so decide your own judgment each time. (x³ is read as "x cubed".)
z-m-24-02.thinking.0: Stating the range (condition) in which an argument holds
z-m-24-02.thinking.1: Revising or keeping a judgment with new information
z-m-24-02.thinking.2: Writing an answer that depends on the range
z-m-24-02.thinking.3: Finding several solutions yourself and verifying them
z-m-24-02.prereq.0: H2 in this batch is a division of difficulty and support level and does not mean the grade taught at school. Assumed school order: you have already learned in Common Math the meaning of complex numbers (the imaginary unit i, i² = −1) and their multiplication, the discriminant of quadratic equations, and factoring of cubic expressions.
z-m-24-02.prereq.1: The condition for two complex numbers to be equal: the real parts are equal to each other, and the imaginary parts are equal to each other.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose a judgment and look at whether the new information changes or keeps the judgment.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information comes out, reread the choice you made earlier and write in one line what changed.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.hint.1: Before choosing an option, first look at "which range of numbers" that choice assumes.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.info: This is a problem of solving the equation x³ = 1. The range of x is not written in the problem. Minsu's solution: "x = 1 is a solution. If x > 1 then x³ > 1, and if x < 1 then x³ < 1, so the only solution is x = 1." ('>' is read as "is greater than" and '<' is read as "is less than".)
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you judge Minsu's solution?
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.after: If x is a real number, Minsu's argument is correct (if it is greater than 1, x³ > 1, and if less, x³ < 1). But the range is not written, so we cannot yet know whether thinking only about real numbers is enough.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: All numbers can be compared in size, so Minsu's solution is correct and the only solution is 1
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You did not consider whether all numbers can be lined up as greater and less. Think about which numbers can be compared in size.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The solution is correct when x is a real number. But there is no range, so more checking is needed
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You read which numbers the solution assumes, and also included in your judgment that the range is missing.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: A cubic equation must have three solutions, so a solution that says there is one is wrong
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You asserted the number of solutions from the degree alone. How many different solutions there are has to be checked by looking at the expression and the range.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: You only plugged in x = 1, so nothing can be known from this solution
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The solution also has a part that considers the cases greater than 1 and less than 1. Read what that part guarantees.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Two new pieces of information have come out. (1) x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1), and the discriminant of the quadratic equation x² + x + 1 = 0 is 1 − 4 = −3. (2) The explanation at the front of this problem book says "in this unit, equations are solved in the complex numbers", but this problem itself still has no range.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now how would you answer "how many different solutions are there"?
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.after: From x − 1 = 0 the real solution 1 comes out, and x² + x + 1 = 0 has a negative discriminant, so it has no real solutions and has two different imaginary solutions. If real, 1 solution; if complex, 3 solutions. Since the range is not settled, both answering by range, or writing the assumption based on the unit explanation and answering 3, are reasonable. Minsu's judgment "in the real numbers there is one solution" stays as it is.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The problem has no range, so think only of real numbers and answer only that the solution is 1
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It is correct as an answer in the real number range, but you did not use the new information, the discriminant calculation and the unit explanation, in your judgment.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The discriminant is −3, which is negative, so this equation has no solutions in any range of numbers
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The discriminant is information about the one factor x² + x + 1. You forgot that there is another factor, x − 1.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Answer by splitting the range: 1 solution if real, 3 solutions if complex
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You put the fact that the range is not settled into the answer as it is. This judgment shows that the answer depends on the conditions.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Following the unit explanation, treat it as complex and write 3, while stating the assumption
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You used the clue of the unit explanation and stated the assumption. This judgment wrote both the basis and the limit.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Call one imaginary root ω = (−1 + √3 i)/2. (i is the imaginary unit with i² = −1, and the expression is read as "minus 1 plus root 3 i, over 2".) We know that ω is a root of x² + x + 1 = 0. We want to check directly whether this ω really also satisfies x³ = 1.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which methods of checking are valid? (There may be several methods.)
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Both methods are exact checks. a uses only ω² + ω + 1 = 0, and c finds ω² directly and multiplies. An approximate value (b) is only a check that catches calculation mistakes and not a confirmation, and d assumes the conclusion in advance. Since the imaginary root also satisfies x³ = 1 in this way, the earlier judgment that there are 3 solutions in the complex numbers is supported.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Use ω² = −ω − 1 to calculate ω³ = ω·ω² = −ω² − ω = 1
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You chose the way of lowering ω³ to a linear expression in ω using an expression you already know.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Write ω as −0.5 + 0.87i, multiply several times, and consider it checked if it is close to 1
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Calculating with approximate values helps as a check, but it does not confirm that it is exactly 1.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Find ω² and multiply by ω to check that (−1+√3 i)(−1−√3 i)/4 = 1
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You chose the way of checking by multiplying directly. The key is how the imaginary part disappears.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Since ω is a root of some equation, regard ω³ = 1 as already holding and use it as it is
z-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You assumed the conclusion you want to check to be already true. The equation of which ω is a root is x² + x + 1 = 0, not x³ = 1.
z-m-24-02.s.s1.reflect: If you first thought "the only solution is 1", what information narrowed that judgment to "correct in the real numbers"? Why can the argument that compares sizes not be used for imaginary numbers?
z-m-24-02.s.s2.prompt: Suppose a complex number z = a + bi (a, b are real numbers) satisfies z³ = 1. Since (a + bi)³ = (a³ − 3ab²) + (3a²b − b³)i, the real part a³ − 3ab² must be 1 and the imaginary part 3a²b − b³ must be 0. Enter 3 different solutions as (a, b). Irrational numbers may be written rounded to two decimal places, and an error within 0.02 is accepted.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.hint.0: Check what x³ − 1 becomes when you plug in z = 1, and find the roots of the remaining quadratic expression x² + x + 1.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put the real part of the root you found in a and the number in front of i in b, and calculate whether the two expressions are close to 1 and 0, respectively.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.var.b: b (the number in front of i)
z-m-24-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The real part matches 1 (within an error of 0.02).
z-m-24-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The real part a³ − 3ab² of (a + bi)³ is not 1.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The imaginary part matches 0 (within an error of 0.02).
z-m-24-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The imaginary part 3a²b − b³ of (a + bi)³ is not 0.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.explain: The solutions are the three, z = 1, z = (−1 + √3 i)/2, z = (−1 − √3 i)/2. As decimals they are about (1, 0), (−0.5, 0.87), (−0.5, −0.87). The same solution written with different digits after the decimal point is not counted as a different solution. The only solution whose imaginary part is 0 is 1, and by comparing sizes alone you cannot find the other two solutions.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why Minsu's argument "if it is greater than 1, x³ > 1, and if less, x³ < 1" cannot find the imaginary roots, and how many different solutions there are in the real number range and in the complex number range.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Point out which numbers are assumed where 'x > 1' or 'x < 1' is used in Minsu's argument.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Split into the real number range and the complex number range and count the solutions you found earlier in each.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write in your own words that Minsu's argument relies on "which numbers can be compared in size"?
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write both the number of solutions in the real number range and the number in the complex number range?
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think about the imaginary roots by connecting them with the values you found above (real part −0.5 and so on)?
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.model.0: Minsu's solution is right only when x is a real number. Sizes can be compared only between real numbers, and imaginary numbers cannot be ordered by size, so imaginary roots cannot be found by this method. In the real number range there is 1 solution, and in the complex number range there are 3.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.model.1: In the complex number range, Minsu's argument cannot be used. Imaginary numbers have no greater or less, so you cannot reason with inequality signs. If real, there is one (1), and if complex, there are three: 1 and two imaginary roots.
z-m-24-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: It said the condition for comparing sizes with the expression "cannot reason with inequality signs".
